q: How well does the Coppersmith QFT circuit, drop-in replaced for the paper's Eq. 11 pulse program, reproduce the reported 87 percent overall NMR fidelity when composed with a realistic amplitude-damping + phase-damping channel calibrated to the paper's T1=1.56 s and T2=420 ms on alanine C-13 at 100.6 MHz, rather than an isotropic depolarizing channel?
basis: The paper's overall F=87 percent is dominated by two effects it separates by hand: RF-pulse imperfection and coherent-decay attenuation. Our ideal statevector rules out the algorithmic-decomposition contribution to that gap, but we did not run a T1/T2 open-system simulation that would tell us how much of the 13-point fidelity deficit is coherent-error vs decoherence in the specific 3-qubit alanine setting.
next_steps: Rebuild the six-gate sequence in qiskit-aer with a per-qubit thermal_relaxation_error parameterised by T1=1.56 s, T2=420 ms, and durations set by 1/(8*Jij) (54, 35, 1.2 Hz) for each B-gate delay; report F(rho_theory, rho_exp) via Eq. 12 and compare to 87 percent.

q: The paper claims per-gate F > 98 percent after renormalizing rho_exp to compensate for the decoherence-driven attenuation. Under what noise model is that renormalization actually valid (i.e., under which noise channels does the QFT act as an isotropic scalar on the deviation density matrix), and does that assumption hold for anisotropic J13=1.2 Hz coupling errors that require long refocusing intervals?
basis: During the replication we noticed that J13 is 30x-45x smaller than J12/J23, so 1/(8*J13) refocusing intervals are ~100 ms, comparable to T2. That makes the 'decoherence uniformly attenuates the deviation matrix' approximation quantitatively suspect, but the paper uses it to lift F from 87 percent to 98 percent per gate.
next_steps: Simulate the six-gate sequence with (a) depolarizing noise and (b) T1/T2 noise on a per-interval basis, apply the paper's renormalization to rho_exp, and check whether the isotropic-attenuation approximation reproduces the correct rho_theory overlap for both noise types.

q: The paper skips SWAPs by 'reordering the bits at the appropriate interval'. What is the exact bit-labeling map from the input NMR spins (carbonyl, C-alpha, C-beta) to the qubit indices in Eq. 11, and does that relabeling propagate into the spectra shown in Figure 1?
basis: Our Coppersmith circuit needs an explicit SWAP-based bit reversal to match Qiskit's little-endian ordering; the paper avoids it via relabeling, but does not print the permutation. That ambiguity blocks a bit-for-bit reproduction of Fig 1's assignment of A/B/C spectra to qubit indices.
next_steps: Construct all 6 possible bit-permutations of the QFT_3 output for a given input, and match each against the paper's Fig 1 A/B/C peak assignments (magnitudes of density-matrix off-diagonals) to pin down the intended qubit->spin mapping.

q: For n up to what qubit count does the Coppersmith n(n-1)/2 controlled-phase count remain the minimum-depth QFT decomposition on an all-to-all-connected qubit register, before approximate-QFT (dropping small-angle B-gates) or nearest-neighbor-only architectures change the optimum?
basis: We verified the H=n, CP=n(n-1)/2 counts exactly for n=3,4,5. But the paper's smallest B-gate has angle pi/2^(L-1) which for L=3 is pi/4 -- still large. Approximate QFTs drop small-angle B-gates for depth reduction with bounded error; the scaling of that tradeoff is not explored here.
next_steps: Sweep n=3..12 with (a) full Coppersmith and (b) approximate-QFT truncated to k largest B-gates per Hadamard; report Frobenius distance vs full QFT and gate-count vs k.

q: Our ideal-statevector reproduction of QFT_3 |x> for x in {0,1,3,7} matches the analytic formula to ~1e-15. On real 2026-era superconducting or trapped-ion hardware with per-two-qubit-gate error ~1e-3, what n is the crossover where a full Coppersmith QFT stops being distinguishable from a Haar-random unitary via a state-tomography F metric like Eq. 12?
basis: The paper reports 87 percent overall fidelity on 3 qubits with 1990s NMR. We showed the algorithmic decomposition is exact; the only knob left is hardware error. This raises the question of how many qubits modern hardware can support before per-gate error accumulation forces F below a Haar-random baseline for the QFT specifically.
next_steps: Simulate n=3..20 QFT with per-CP-gate depolarizing error eps in {1e-4,1e-3,1e-2}, compute F vs analytic per Eq. 12, and find n* such that F(n*) equals the Haar-random baseline 1/2 + 1/(2*sqrt(2^n)).
